title: Data and sources
text:
Dataset: Billboard Hot 100 weekly charts, 2 August 1958 to 29 May 2021, from TidyTuesday, 14 September 2021 (compiled by Sean Miller from Billboard.com).
Transformations, limitations and rule changes go here.
To reproduce: run R/01_download.R, then R/02_clean.R, then render the site.

title: Are hits getting more disposable?
text:
Story summary goes here.

Version A: Scientific article
Version B: Web explainer
Data and sources

title: Version A: Scientific article
text:
A common claim about the streaming era is that popular music has become more disposable: songs rise quickly and are forgotten just as fast. Weekly Billboard Hot 100 charts allow this claim to be examined over six decades. I collapsed 327,895 weekly chart entries into one record per song and measured each song’s longevity as its total number of weeks on the chart, counting re-entries, for the 28,122 songs that debuted between 1959 and 2019.
Figure 1 shows the median chart run by year of debut. Longevity rose steadily for four decades, from roughly 7–9 weeks in the 1960s to a peak of 20 weeks for songs debuting in 2001, before falling sharply to a median of 4 weeks in 2019. Taken at face value, this trajectory supports the disposability claim. However, the distribution around the median suggests that this reading is incomplete: from 1991 onward, the upper quartile is fixed at almost exactly 20 weeks, a ceiling that coincides with a change in Billboard’s chart methodology. We examine this pattern in the following section.








Figure 1: Median number of weeks spent on the Billboard Hot 100, by year of chart debut (N = 28,122 songs, 1959–2019). The shaded band shows the interquartile range (25th–75th percentile). Weeks are counted across all chart runs, including re-entries. The dashed line marks the 1991 introduction of Billboard’s recurrent rule, which removes songs from the chart after 20 weeks once they fall below No. 50.

title: Version A: Scientific article
section: Two discontinuities in the distribution of chart runs
text:
Two discontinuities in the distribution of chart runs
Medians summarise the centre of a distribution but can conceal discontinuities within it. Figure 2 therefore shows the full distribution of chart-run lengths for songs debuting in three periods: before the 1991 methodology change (1959–1990), after the change but before digital downloads became widespread (1991–2004), and the download and streaming era (2010–2019). Songs debuting 2005–2009 are omitted as a transition period.
Before 1991, chart runs follow a smooth, right-skewed distribution: runs of exactly 20 weeks account for 2% of songs, no different from neighbouring lengths. Among songs debuting in 1991–2004, 25% leave the chart at exactly 20 weeks. This discontinuity corresponds to Billboard’s recurrent rule, introduced in 1991, which removes a song from the Hot 100 once it has charted for 20 weeks and fallen below No. 50. Consistent with this mechanism, 92% of the 1,119 songs in this period with runs of exactly 20 weeks were positioned below No. 50 in their final chart week.
A second discontinuity appears in 2010–2019, when 28% of songs (1,245 of 4,446) spend a single week on the chart, compared with 3% before 1991. These entries are overwhelmingly marginal: 91% never rose above No. 50, with a median peak position of No. 81. They reflect a release pattern in which tracks from newly released albums briefly enter the chart on first-week downloads or streams; in 2010–2011 they also include a large number of Glee cast recordings (12% of all one-week entries in the decade). Together, these two features account for much of the trajectory in Figure 1. The rise in median longevity after 1991 coincides with a policy-imposed ceiling, while the decline after 2005 is driven largely by a growing mass of single-week entries at the bottom of the chart.








Figure 2: Distribution of total weeks on the Billboard Hot 100 for songs debuting in three periods. Bars show the share of each period’s songs with a given chart run; runs longer than 40 weeks are not shown. Black bars mark runs of exactly 1 and exactly 20 weeks, with their shares labelled. Songs debuting 2005–2009 are omitted as a transition period.

title: Version A: Scientific article
section: Top hits have grown more durable
text:
Top hits have grown more durable
If median chart longevity is shaped by a policy ceiling and by a growing number of marginal single-week entries, a fairer test of the disposability claim requires a measure that neither affects. We therefore restricted the analysis to songs that peaked in the Top 10 (n = 4,837) and measured how many weeks each spent in the Top 40. The recurrent rule applies only to songs below No. 50, and single-week entries almost never reach the Top 10: of the 1,245 one-week songs debuting in 2010–2019, only one did.
Figure 3 compares this measure with the all-song median from Figure 1. The two series track each other closely until the early 2000s, then diverge. While the median song’s total chart run fell, Top 10 hits continued to grow more durable: their median time in the Top 40 rose from 10 weeks for songs debuting in the 1960s to 13 weeks in the 1980s, 21 weeks in the 2000s and 24 weeks in the 2010s. Consistent with longer stays at the top, fewer songs reached the Top 10 each year, falling from an average of about 106 per year in the 1960s to about 52 per year in the 2010s.
One caveat applies. Top 10 longevity also rises sharply around 1991, from a median of 13 weeks for songs debuting in 1985–1990 to 20 weeks for those debuting in 1992–1997. Because the recurrent rule does not affect songs in the Top 40, this jump more likely reflects Billboard’s concurrent adoption of Nielsen SoundScan sales data and Broadcast Data Systems (BDS) airplay monitoring, which replaced reported store and radio surveys. Part of the long-run increase may therefore reflect improved measurement rather than changes in listening behaviour alone.
Taken together, the three figures suggest that the Hot 100 has not become uniformly more disposable. The bottom of the chart now turns over faster than at any point in its history, but the songs at the top remain there longer than ever. Apparent trends in chart longevity depend substantially on how the chart itself is constructed.








Figure 3: Median weeks by year of chart debut for two measures. Dashed grey: total weeks on the chart for all songs (as in Figure 1). Solid black: weeks spent in the Top 40 for songs that peaked in the Top 10 (n = 4,837). The Top 40 measure is unaffected by the recurrent rule, which applies only below No. 50, and by one-week entries, which rarely reach the Top 10. Dotted line: 1991, when the recurrent rule was introduced and Billboard began using Nielsen SoundScan sales and BDS airplay data.

title: Are hit songs getting more disposable?
text:
It feels like songs come and go faster than ever. A track blows up on TikTok, everyone streams it for a week, and then it’s gone. The Billboard Hot 100 has ranked America’s most popular songs every week since 1958, so we can check whether that feeling is true.
We looked at 28,122 songs that hit the chart between 1959 and 2019 and asked a simple question: how long did each one stay?

title: Are hit songs getting more disposable?
section: At first glance, yes: songs are vanishing faster
text:
At first glance, yes: songs are vanishing faster
In the 1960s, a typical song spent about 7 weeks on the Hot 100. That number climbed for 40 years, to a high of 20 weeks in 2001. Then it crashed. By 2019, the typical song lasted just 4 weeks.
Hover over the line to see any year.








Figure 1




Case closed? Not quite. Something odd is hiding underneath that line.

title: Are hit songs getting more disposable?
section: But two “walls” in the data weren’t built by listeners
text:
But two “walls” in the data weren’t built by listeners
Instead of looking at the typical song, let’s count how many songs lasted exactly 1 week, exactly 2 weeks, and so on. If people simply lose interest at different times, you’d expect a smooth curve. That’s exactly what we see before 1991.
After that, two strange walls appear.








Figure 2





The 20-week wall is a rule. In 1991, Billboard started removing any song that had been on the chart for 20 weeks once it dropped below No. 50, to make room for new music. Songs didn’t stop being popular at week 20. Billboard stopped counting them.
The one-week wall is about how music is released now. When a big artist drops an album, many of its tracks get streamed enough to chart in the first week, then fall off. Nine in ten of them never make it into the top half of the chart. In 2020, 15 Taylor Swift album tracks did exactly this.
So that first chart was measuring Billboard’s rules and album release days as much as what people actually liked.

title: Are hit songs getting more disposable?
section: The biggest hits are lasting longer than ever
text:
The biggest hits are lasting longer than ever
Here’s a fairer test. Take only the songs that became real hits by reaching the Top 10, and count how long they stayed in the Top 40. Neither wall touches this: the 20-week rule only removes songs below No. 50, and one-week album tracks almost never reach the Top 10.
Hover over either line to compare years.








Figure 3




The two lines move together for decades, then split apart. The typical song now disappears in a few weeks, but the biggest hits are staying near the top longer than ever: about 10 weeks in the 1960s, 26 weeks by 2019.

title: Are hit songs getting more disposable?
section: So, are hits getting more disposable?
text:
So, are hits getting more disposable?
No, but the chart has changed shape. The bottom of the Hot 100 now churns faster than ever, with dozens of songs passing through for a single week. The top has become stickier: the songs everyone really listens to stay there for months.
Whether music looks “disposable” depends on which songs you count and on rules most listeners never hear about.






NoteHow we measured this (click to expand)






Data: every weekly Billboard Hot 100 chart from August 1958 to May 2021, via TidyTuesday. We counted each song once and added up all its weeks on the chart, including re-entries.
“Typical song” means the median: half of songs lasted longer, half shorter. We used the median because a few songs that lasted over a year would distort an average.
Years: songs that first charted from 1959 to 2019. Songs from 2020 on hadn’t finished their chart runs when the data ends.
One more change in 1991: Billboard also switched to electronic sales and radio tracking (Nielsen SoundScan and BDS) that year. That’s probably why Top 10 hits jump in the early 1990s, so part of their rise reflects better measurement, not only listener behaviour.
Full technical details are in the scientific version.
